analysis.one_liner: Caps sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide emissions from the nation's power plants.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to cap four major power plant pollutants — including carbon dioxide — never got a hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set declining national limits on four pollutants from fossil-fuel power plants: sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and, for the first time, carbon dioxide. Power plants would comply by buying, selling, and banking emission allowances under a cap-and-trade system. It also tightened rules for aging plants and ordered regular air quality forecasts. It never left the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People downwind of coal-fired power plants, who breathe sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury; states dealing with acid rain, smog, and mercury in fish; and renewable energy and nuclear operators, who would receive allowances or credits under the new programs.

how_it_helps.text: Caps sulfur dioxide emissions from affected power plants at 4,500,000 tons per year for 2010-2014 and 2,000,000 tons per year from 2015 onward.
Sets declining nitrogen oxide caps, with 1,300,000 tons per year for eastern Zone 1 states and 320,000 tons for Zone 2 states beginning in 2015.
Requires coal plants to capture 60 percent of inlet mercury in 2010-2014 and 90 percent from 2015 onward, with a $50,000-per-day-per-pound penalty for excess emissions.

Establishes the first federal cap on carbon dioxide from power plants, holding emissions at projected 2006 levels through 2014 and returning to 2001 levels from 2015 onward, with a trading program and offsets.
Directs NOAA to issue air quality forecasts and warnings for every region of the country.
Requires EPA to set limits on hazardous air pollutants from utility steam generating units other than mercury.

analysis.who_pays: Coal-fired power plant owners and operators, who would face allowance costs and pollution control requirements, and their customers to the extent those costs are passed through to electricity rates.

drawbacks.text: Allowances are handed out free to existing plants based on their past output, and a reserve is set aside to subsidize 'clean coal' technologies, so polluters would receive billions in allowances rather than paying the public for them.

The carbon dioxide cap only returns emissions to 2001 levels by 2015 — a modest cut by climate standards — and the bill guarantees no tightening of any cap for at least a decade after enactment, subjecting the limits to a review only after ten years.

Performance standards under the new source review program would not apply to old plants until 2020 and only to units operating 50 or more years, leaving many aging polluters largely untouched for years.
A cost an honest supporter would acknowledge: compliance costs would ultimately flow into electricity rates, hitting households in coal-dependent states hardest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver large, verifiable public health and environmental gains — steep cuts in soot, smog, mercury, and the first-ever national carbon cap — through a system that traded away some strength to win utility and coal-state support: free allowances, a clean coal subsidy, and a decade-long freeze on tightening the caps. It is a genuine improvement over the status quo, but a compromise version of strong policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on May 4, 2006 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which took no further action on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Carper introduced the bill on May 4, 2006, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
Seven senators from both parties — four Republicans and three Democrats — signed on as cosponsors.
The committee never reported the bill, held no vote, and the full Senate never considered it; the action history shows no activity after the initial referral.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, killing the bill; similar Carper multi-pollutant proposals were reintroduced in later Congresses.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of coal-fired power plants and the coal industry came out ahead: they avoided mandatory caps on sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide for the remainder of the Congress, while the public continued to bear the pollution.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal plant owners and coal interests

for.name: Sen. Thomas R. Carper
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and negotiated a bipartisan multi-pollutant compromise capping four power plant pollutants.

for.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as an original co-sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Christopher Dodd, Dianne Feinstein, and Lindsey Graham
for.role: U.S. Senators from Connecticut, California, and South Carolina
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it three Democrats and four Republicans in total.

against.name: Sen. James Inhofe
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: As the committee chairman who controlled the agenda, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: President George W. Bush administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory carbon dioxide caps on power plants and promoted its own voluntary-oriented multi-pollutant plan instead of binding carbon limits.

against.name: Coal and electric utility interests
against.role: Coal mining companies and coal-fired utilities
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory carbon dioxide caps that would raise the cost of burning coal, favoring weaker or voluntary approaches.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — four Republicans and three Democrats signed on — but the committee that buried the bill was chaired by a Republican who rejected mandatory carbon limits, so the roadblock was partisan even if the bill was not.

industries.note: The bill would impose real caps and compliance costs on coal plants, cutting their pollution sharply. But it would hand them free allowances based on past output, create a reserve to subsidize 'clean coal' technologies, and guarantee no tighter caps for a decade — locking coal generation into the emission-trading system as a permanent, compensated participant.

Mandatory caps on carbon dioxide and mercury would reduce the demand and ease for burning coal in power plants. The industry's interest in avoiding these caps ran against the public's interest in cleaner air.
Nuclear units built before 1991 would receive carbon allowances for generation above their 1990 levels, giving operators a valuable asset for expanding output as fossil generation was capped.
Wind, biomass, solar, hydro, geothermal, and fuel cell generators would be covered units eligible for allowances, and the bill lists encouraging renewable energy among its purposes.

industries.industry: Pollution control and monitoring equipment makers
industries.note: Mandatory requirements for continuous monitoring of nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide would create demand for monitoring systems and scrubber technology at hundreds of plants.
